title: The Weaver and Drama Artist Who Stopped Speaking Clearly — A Missed Follow-Up, a Delayed Return, and a Widening Diagnosis

sections.heading: The Patient's Story
sections.content:
He is 65 years old, a handloom weaver and drama artist by trade, though he stopped working two years ago. He came in with lower backache going back five years. Two years ago, his mother died, and he fell into a depression — low mood and frequent crying that lasted about four months.

Eighteen months before this admission, he suddenly had difficulty getting up from a squatting position and was rushed to hospital. There was no slurred speech, no falls, no giddiness, no involuntary movements, and no bowel or bladder incontinence at that time. An MRI suggested possible infarcts, and his attenders were told he might have joint disease or a clot in the brain, with instructions to review in 15 days — but the COVID lockdown meant that follow-up never happened.

Since then he has needed a stick to walk, has had trouble getting up from sitting, has lost memory, cannot participate in active conversation, and cannot express his feelings — all gradually worsening, though without sleep disturbance. One week before this admission, things sharpened: high-grade fever with chills and rigors, a productive cough he couldn't expectorate (he swallowed the sputum instead), worsening shortness of breath after coughing, reduced food and liquid intake, difficulty swallowing, and drooling of food and saliva. He has had diabetes for five years (on glimepiride/metformin combination) and hypertension for ten years (on cilnidipine), and has smoked heavily for 50 years, more recently cutting down from 1.5 packs of beedis a day to 3–4.

sections.heading: What the Work-Up Showed So Far
sections.content:
- General exam: no pallor, icterus, cyanosis, clubbing, lymphadenopathy, or pedal edema
- Vitals: temperature 98.6°F, pulse 103 bpm, respiratory rate 20/min, blood pressure 130/90 mmHg, oxygen saturation 95% on room air
- Neurological exam: not oriented to time, place, or person; slurred speech; mouth deviated to the left, indicating right facial weakness, with an intact gag reflex; tone increased in both upper limbs, normal in the lower limbs; power reduced to 3/5 in both upper limbs and 2/5 in both lower limbs, with full hand grip; reflexes brisk (3+) at the biceps, triceps, supinator, and knees, normal (2+) at the ankles, with extensor plantar responses on both sides; sensory and cerebellar exam could not be assessed given his mental status; equivocal neck rigidity, meningeal signs otherwise negative
- Cardiorespiratory and abdominal exam: unremarkable
- Investigations sent: hemogram, urine examination, complete blood picture, liver and renal function tests, ECG, chest X-ray, ultrasound abdomen, MRI brain, and MRI whole-spine screening

Working diagnosis: compressive myelopathy, an acute infarct in the left anterior temporal lobe, possible spondyloarthropathy, and vascular dementia (possible multi-infarct dementia).

sections.heading: How the Story Unfolded on the Ward
sections.content:
He was started on nasogastric tube feeding, intravenous fluids, and aspirin-atorvastatin combination therapy, with temperature charting. His fever and cough did not resolve immediately, and his blood glucose was found markedly elevated (361 mg/dL) the following day, prompting the addition of ceftriaxone (Monocef), sliding-scale insulin, and closer glucose monitoring.

Over the following days his fever and cough gradually subsided, though he remained disoriented to time, place, and person throughout, with his facial weakness, slurred speech, and limb findings essentially unchanged. His blood pressure ran variably high. His regimen was built out further with clopidogrel added to his aspirin, insulin adjusted to a fixed pre-meal schedule, baclofen and lactulose started, and nursing measures — frequent repositioning and topical antibiotic powder — added once bed sores were noted, alongside continued physiotherapy for both lower limbs. Through the last several days documented, his clinical picture and working diagnosis remained stable and unchanged, with fever and cough resolved and his neurological deficits persisting without further acute change.
